item.title: Moving a non-EU employee from your Nordic office to Italy: the permit process
item.description: Nordic citizens move freely to Italy. Your non-EU engineers do not. EU Blue Card, quota permits under the 2026–2028 Decreto Flussi, and the steps in order.

item.title: Unions in Italy for Nordic employers: less negotiation, more agreement
item.description: Nordic companies are used to local union cooperation. In Italy, unions act mainly through national agreements. What a small foreign employer actually meets.

item.title: Sales staff in Italy and permanent establishment risk for Nordic companies
item.description: An Italian seller can create a taxable presence for your Nordic company. When the risk arises, what reduces it, and how it affects the choice of EOR or entity.

item.title: When should a Nordic company move from EOR to its own Italian company?
item.description: The signals that it is time to set up an Italian srl or branch, what the move involves, and how employees transfer without losing seniority.

item.title: Recruiting Italian developers for a Nordic scale-up
item.description: Why Nordic tech companies hire developers in Italy, where to find them, how to run the process, and what makes them say yes to a foreign employer.

item.title: Life sciences in Italy for Danish, Swedish and Finnish biotech and medtech
item.description: Where Italy's clinical, regulatory and medical affairs talent is, which roles Nordic life sciences companies hire first, and what to watch for compliance.

item.title: Bologna and the Packaging Valley: field engineers for Nordic machinery companies
item.description: Emilia-Romagna is a centre of packaging, food-processing and automation machinery. How Nordic equipment makers hire service and applications engineers there.

item.title: Turin for Nordic vehicle and component makers: hiring automotive engineers
item.description: Why Turin suits Swedish and Finnish vehicle, truck and component companies, what talent is there, how local tax works and how to hire without an entity.

item.title: Making a job offer in Italy that closes: a guide for Nordic hiring managers
item.description: Italian candidates compare RAL, net pay, stability and benefits. How a Nordic company without an Italian office can make an offer that gets signed.

item.title: Flat hierarchy meets Italian workplace culture: feedback and decisions
item.description: Nordic managers lead by consensus and understatement. Italian colleagues often expect clearer direction and warmer contact. Practical habits for mixed teams.

item.title: July at home, August in Italy: planning holiday coverage across both calendars
item.description: Nordic offices empty in July, Italian ones in August. How to use the offset, plan public holidays and keep customers covered all summer.

item.title: Productivity bonuses in Italy: the 1% flat tax Nordic employers should know
item.description: In 2026 Italian productivity bonuses up to €5,000 a year can be taxed at 1% under a qualifying company plan. How it works and how it differs from a normal bonus.

item.title: Lunch benefit, Italian style: meal vouchers and fringe benefits in 2026
item.description: Electronic meal vouchers are tax-free up to €10 a day in Italy in 2026; fringe benefits up to €1,000 a year, €2,000 with children. How Nordic employers use them.

item.title: Reading an Italian payslip (busta paga) as a Nordic manager
item.description: The Italian payslip has more lines than a Swedish lönespecifikation. What each block means, so you can answer your employee and check the invoice.

item.title: RAL vs månadslön: how Italian candidates talk about salary
item.description: Nordic offers quote a monthly salary. Italian offers quote RAL, gross annual pay in 13 or 14 instalments. How to state, compare and negotiate an offer.

item.title: Converting your Italian consultant into an employee
item.description: Your Italian freelancer has become part of the team. Why that is a risk, and how to move them onto an Italian employment contract through an EOR.

item.title: EOR, freelancer or Italian subsidiary: three routes for a Nordic company
item.description: How a Swedish, Danish, Norwegian or Finnish company can have people working in Italy: an Employer of Record, a freelancer, or its own srl. Pros, risks, timing.

item.title: Fixed-term or permanent in Italy? A decision guide for Nordic employers
item.description: Italy, like Sweden, treats the open-ended contract as the norm. When a fixed-term contract fits, when it backfires, and what it means for retention.

item.title: Non-compete clauses in Italy: why a Nordic template will not survive
item.description: Italian non-competes are valid only if written, paid and limited in time, place and activity. What Nordic employers must change in their standard clause.

item.title: Remote work in Italy: the written lavoro agile agreement Nordic companies need
item.description: A remote-first Nordic company cannot rely on a policy page in Italy. Lavoro agile needs a written agreement. What it must cover and how to prepare it.

item.title: Working hours, overtime and disconnection in Italy: a guide for Nordic teams
item.description: Same time zone, different rules: how Italian working time, overtime and the right to disconnect work, and how a Nordic team can schedule without friction.

item.title: Sick leave in Italy for Nordic managers: no karensavdrag, a different certificate
item.description: In Sweden the employer pays 80% sick pay for 14 days after a qualifying deduction. In Italy the doctor certifies online to INPS. What a manager may ask.

item.title: Employer contributions: Sweden 31.42%, Norway 14.1%, Italy around 30%
item.description: The same gross salary costs different amounts in Stockholm, Oslo and Milan. How Italian employer and employee contributions and income tax compare with home.

item.title: The 13th month: why Italian salaries come in more than twelve parts
item.description: Nordic payroll has twelve salaries a year. Italian payroll has thirteen, sometimes fourteen. What the extra months are and how to keep cash flow flat.

item.title: Occupational pension at home, INPS and TFR in Italy: the pension layer explained
item.description: Nordic employers fund pensions through statutory and agreement-based schemes. In Italy the employer pays 23.81% for the state pension, plus the TFR. How to budget it.

item.title: Parental leave: from 480 Swedish days to the Italian model
item.description: Nordic parental leave is long and shared. Italy has a compulsory maternity period, a short paternity leave and optional leave on top. How to plan the team.

item.title: 25 days at home, four weeks in Italy: how Italian holiday really adds up
item.description: Nordic employees get 25 days of holiday by law. Italian law says four weeks, but collective agreements add hours off. What Nordic HR should plan for.

item.title: Provanställning vs periodo di prova: probation in Italy for Nordic employers
item.description: Swedish and Italian probation both run up to six months. The Italian version has stricter form rules and ends without notice. What to set up before day one.

item.title: LAS vs Italian dismissal rules: what a Swedish employer should expect
item.description: Both Sweden and Italy require a valid reason to dismiss. The grounds, the notice and the procedure differ. A practical comparison for Nordic HR teams.

item.title: Italian CCNL vs Swedish kollektivavtal: same idea, different default
item.description: Swedish managers know collective agreements. The Italian CCNL works on a similar logic, with one big difference: it applies from the first hire.
